correctness.rationale: The piecewise formula matches C^2 at both interfaces; has zero boundary values and the strict sign needed for the rate selector; satisfies the Bellman identity exactly on every region; and an integrable stopped Dynkin argument proves a bound against all predictable rate controls. Equality for the proposed feedback proves global optimality. A separate tridiagonal policy iteration checker confirmed 60 finite-state analogues and 11,260 value comparisons. Finite tests are secondary to the complete analytic proof.

evidence: Aspman et al. analyze piecewise prescribed reset rates for potential-driven diffusion and a single target, not arbitrary feedback policies with two absorbing endpoints.
Pal et al. analyze unconditional and conditional absorption under constant Poisson resetting in a finite interval.
broader_coverage.reasoning: The papers provide overlapping models or equations, but their stated hypotheses/conclusions do not optimize over every bounded spatially and history-dependent rate for the two-exit criterion. The present result is not merely a numerical parameter extension of their fixed-policy formulas.

evidence: Evans–Majumdar Section 3.2 has an optimal infinite-rate rule in the presence of one known absorbing target and evaluates a symmetric nonresetting window, not the optimal finite-rate two-exit mirror window.

De Bruyne–Mori prove the general bang-bang control principle but do not solve an exit-time reward for two absorbing boundaries; their Section IV discussion flags first-passage payoffs as further work.
Aspman et al. fix reset-rate profiles before evaluating first-passage time to one target.
Pal et al. equation (17) is the finite-interval constant-reset-rate mean; it does not bound variable spatial policies.
claim_vs_prior_implication.reasoning: None of the inspected results has premises and conclusion strong enough to imply the exact two-exit optimal policy and its rate-independent switching points as a stated corollary without solving the new nonlinear boundary-value problem. The generic HJB equation is a method used in the proof and explicitly credited, not an originality assertion.

evidence: Evans–Majumdar, Section 3.2, gives an immediate-reset half-line control for a known single target and notes a different constrained control remains open.

equivalent_formulations.reasoning: Reflection about the midpoint converts resetting site a to L-a but not the first-exit objective into a one-target half-line problem. The generic Bellman rate comparison identifies the selector given a value function; it does not yield the explicit C^2 solution, its reflected switching coordinates, or its exact mean. Neither alternative statement logically contains the claimed theorem.

value.rationale: Two endpoints create an authentic geometric tradeoff: resetting near an exit loses nearly completed trajectories, whereas resetting in the interior can accelerate escape to either boundary. The exact all-control solution identifies a universal central resetting region with immovable geometric switch positions despite a variable rate ceiling and diffusivity, plus strict benefit, midpoint boundary and strong-ceiling limiting value. This is a complete motivated classification rather than a routine substitution or a tiny numerical improvement.
